power_id text
1 Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration. The present Simon task study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF ; DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT). The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A). The study included three groups: individuals entering prison (incoming group), individuals approaching release (outgoing group), and a community control group included to estimate practice effects associated with repeated testing. A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants. Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses. A preregistered a priori power analysis conducted using GPower (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that a minimum of 45 participants (15 per group) would provide 95% power to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) in the mixed repeated-measures analyses including the community control group. However, GPower approximates mixed withinbetween designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs (Brysbaert, 2019), therefore, additional simulation-based power analysis matched to the mixed-effects models were used here (Supplementary S1, for detailed sample size estimation and recruitment procedure).
2;3;4 These target sample sizes were specified in the preregistration (DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NKDPT) prior to data collection. First, analyses focusing exclusively on incarcerated participants used a mixed repeated-measures design with two groups (incoming vs. outgoing) and six repeated measurements, corresponding to the combination of the three-level Session factor and the two-level Congruency factor (congruent vs. incongruent). Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% statistical power, the required sample size was estimated at 28 participants (14 per group). Second, analyses including the community control group to evaluate practice effects used a mixed repeated-measures design with three groups and four repeated measurements, corresponding to the two-level Session factor and two-level Congruency factor. Under identical assumptions, the required sample size was estimated at 45 participants (15 per group). Finally, because the broader project focused primarily on longitudinal within-person change across three assessment waves, an additional power analysis was conducted separately within each prisoner group. Assuming three sessions and two experimental conditions, this analysis indicated a required sample size of 28 participants per prisoner group. Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.
5 The preregistered target was derived from a priori power analyses in G*Power (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power).
6 However, G*Power approximates these designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions that combine between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), whereas the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models. We therefore conducted an additional simulation-based power analysis for the design actually used; this analysis was not preregistered and was carried out after data collection, and to avoid circularity the effect size was set a priori by convention rather than from the observed estimates. For each candidate sample size, datasets were simulated from a mixed-effects model with the full Group × Session × Congruency structure, a by-participant random intercept, and random slopes for Session and Congruency, with each participant contributing 40 trials per congruency condition and session. The highest-order (Group × Session × Congruency) interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all two-way interactions, and power was defined as the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which this interaction was detected at α = .05, assuming a small three-way interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session-related change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale). For the three-group × twosession design, 80% power was reached at 40 participants per group. Substantially larger baseline samples were therefore recruited to account for the expected attrition.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Marginal Significance

What we found

You described 1 effect with terms related to ‘marginally significant’.

Show details

You described effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’. If p values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a p value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 10 imprecise p values out of 113 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 34 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

README Files

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • 01_MouseTracking.R reads data_Simon_beh.xlsx.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

> read_simon_beh <- function(path, group_override = NULL) {
>   raw <- read_excel(path)
>   # The authoritative Block is the FIRST column, but a CSV export put a byte-order mark on its
>   # header, so R sees it as "﻿Block" rather than "Block". The file also carries a second,
>   # mostly-empty "Block" column and a junk "Session" column. Strip the BOM, then keep only the
>   # FIRST occurrence of each name so `Block` = the real (populated) column and `session` = the
>   # good lowercase one. (NB: the real Block is still genuinely missing for ~45% of S1 trials —
>   # a gap in the source files, not fixable here.)
>   names(raw) <- gsub("﻿", "", names(raw))
>   raw <- raw[, !duplicated(names(raw))]
>   raw %>%
>     rename_with(~ str_replace_all(.x, " ", "_")) %>%
>     mutate(
>       Participant = as.integer(Participant_number), Session = as.integer(session), Trial = as.integer(Trial),
>       Block = suppressWarnings(as.integer(Block)),
>       Group = factor(if (!is.null(group_override)) group_override else Group), Gender = factor(Gender),
>       Congruency = factor(Congruence, levels = c("Congruent", "Incongruent")),
>       Accuracy = as.integer(Accuracy), RT = as.numeric(RT_Choice), Age = as.numeric(Age),
>       TaskOrder = as.integer(TaskOrder), Dir = as.integer(Dir),
>       Pos = as.integer(Pos), Missed = as.character(Missed)
>     ) %>%
>     filter(!is.na(Participant), !is.na(Session), !is.na(Trial), Trial < 81)
> }
> beh_prison <- read_simon_beh(beh_path_prison)

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants completed a mouse-tracking Simon task during EEG recording, allowing conflict to be examined across complementary behavioural, motor, and neural indices.

Participants were recruited as part of a preregistered longitudinal project investigating behavioural and neural adaptations during incarceration.

A total of 350 incarcerated men were recruited across 15 Belgian correctional facilities, including 206 incoming and 144 outgoing participants.

Because the broader project anticipated substantial attrition between assessment waves, considerably larger baseline samples were recruited than required for the planned analyses.

To minimise perceived links between the research and the judicial system, all consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present, and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.

Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks, EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for the experimental session), whereas community controls completed the behavioural tasks with EEG recordings only and received course credits.

One additional outgoing participant completed the post-release follow-up substantially later than planned because of scheduling constraints.

All incarcerated participants were men, whereas the control group comprised 34 women (81.0%) and 8 men (19.0%).

Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming and outgoing participants, and incoming participants were younger than outgoing participants.

During each session, participants completed five computerized cognitive tasks, lasting approximatively one hour while EEG was recorded, followed by 45 minutes of questionnaires for incoming and outgoing participants.

Participants completed a mouse-tracking version of the Simon task adapted from Scherbaum et al. (2010).

On each trial, participants were required to respond to the direction of an arrow while ignoring its spatial location (Fig. 1).

In the first stage of the trial, participants had 1.5 seconds to start the mouse movement upwards.

Upon stimulus presentation, participants had 1 second to click within one of the response boxes.

Participants were excluded if they contributed less than 10 trials per condition or fewer than 30 trials overall.

Because the control group comprised both sexes whereas all incarcerated participants were men, supplementary sensitivity analyses were conducted within the control group to evaluate potential effects of gender on behavioural and neural outcomes (Supplementary S9).

In addition, unlike the standard keypress Simon, Go/No-Go, and stop-signal paradigms used in much of the offender literature (Chen et al., 2005; Pasion et al., 2018; Pasion et al., 2019; Vilà-Balló et al., 2014), the present task presented the Simon stimulus only after participants had initiated mouse movement.

Because the community control group comprised both women (n = 34) and men (n = 8) whereas all incoming and outgoing participants were men, sex was completely confounded with group and could not be entered into the primary between-group models.

Because all incarcerated participants were men, this sex difference could not be modelled across groups.

Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium that varied in security level, detention regime, and capacity.

Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.

Incoming participants were recruited predominantly from Brugge, Nieuw Dendermonde, and Jamioulx, whereas outgoing participants were mainly recruited from Ittre, Leuven Centraal, and Leuze.

Participants were also excluded if they had already been approached during a previous incarceration period.

Incoming participants were additionally excluded if their incarceration was expected to be transient (e.g., imminent release, extradition, or deportation).

To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.

Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.

Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.

At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.

Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming participants (mean difference = 16.23 years, p < .001, d = 1.90) and outgoing participants (mean difference = 23.21 years, p < .001, d = 3.69).

Incoming participants were also significantly younger than outgoing participants (mean difference = 6.97 years, p = .004, d = 0.67).

Participants had to move the cursor to the left or right response box according to the arrow direction while ignoring its spatial location.

Percentage of participants recruited from each prison in the final S1-S2 complete sample, separately for incoming (IN) and outgoing (OUT) participants.

Ethics approval statement:

The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).

manipulated_variables We will manipulate the congruency of the trials, the direction in which the arrows are pointing and the position of the arrows.
missing_data_handling If data are missing on questionnaires, we will replace the missing data by using a multivariate imputation by chained equations algorithm (MICE) which models each feature with missing values as a function of all the other variables, and uses that prediction estimate for imputation (Pedregosa et al., 2011).
additional_comments This study is part of a larger project investigating the changes in executive functions induced by imprisonment and the differential impact of prison regimes. The protocol aims at answering several additional research questions, regarding emotion recognition ability, cognitive control, sensitivity to reward and punishment and anti-social behaviour.
study_type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
blinding No blinding is involved in this study.
randomization We considered the order of the current trial’s arrow direction (left/right) and arrow position (left/right), as well as the previous trial’s arrow direction (left/right) and arrow location (left/right). This resulted in 16 unique trials with 4 combinations for both the current and previous trials. The trial sequence, which consisted of 16 unique trials with 4 combinations for both the current and previous trials, was randomized within each of the 8 blocks.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
research_questions • Previous studies suggest that incarceration may be associated with alterations in cognitive control and self-control (Meijers et al., 2018; Umbach et al., 2018). However, longitudinal evidence remains limited. In addition, although imprisonment may impair cognitive control, it may also support regulation through structure and routine. Hence, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses regarding longitudinal changes in IC.
H1.A: For individuals entering prison (incoming group), incarceration may either strengthen or weaken IC. Specifically, over the course of 8 months, prisoners may (a) show lower accuracy, and longer mouse trajectories on incongruent trials relative to congruent trials; or (b) exhibit the opposite pattern, reflecting improved IC over time.
H1.B: For individuals leaving prison (outgoing group), changes in IC following release may also be bidirectional. Over the course of 8 months after release, former prisoners may (a) show improved IC, reflected by higher accuracy and shorter mouse trajectories on incongruent trials; or (b) exhibit reduced or absent improvement, or even worsening performance, depending on the challenges of reintegration and the duration or quality of prior incarceration.

• At the neural level, response conflict has been associated with increased midfrontal theta activity, particularly during conflict monitoring and cognitive control processes (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2017). In addition, the event-related potential (ERP) evoked by the stimulus usually shows a frontocentral negativity, the N2 component, which is enhanced during conflict monitoring (Yeung et al., 2004) and also when inhibition fails (Ramautar et al., 2004, Dimoska et al., 2006, Smith et al., 2008). Moreover, smaller amplitudes of the positive parietal deflection P3 predict real-world defects in inhibition (Smith et al., 2008, Dimoska et al., 2006, Ramautar et al., 2004).
H2: For both incoming and outgoing groups, we will examine whether neural indices of inhibitory control change longitudinally. Given the absence of strong longitudinal EEG evidence in prison populations, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses. Specifically, we predict that over time, individuals may exhibit either an increase or a decrease in cognitive conflict on incongruent trials, as reflected by changes in response-locked midfrontal theta activity, and in stimulus-locked N2 and P3 amplitudes.
H2.B: Importantly, we expect that these effects may follow different trajectories in incoming and outgoing groups.
study_design_overview The study is a repeated-measures design with time as a within-subject factor (Baseline, 4 months, 8 months). Participants include both incoming detainees assessed shortly after incarceration and outgoing detainees assessed prior to release, recruited from French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. In addition, a community control group is included to account for repeated task exposure effects, with one 4-month interval re-test only. Incoming participants are recruited within the first three to seven weeks following incarceration, whereas outgoing participants are assessed a month prior to release. All incoming and outgoing participants are followed longitudinally at 4- and 8-month intervals.
Participants will complete a Simon Task with mouse-tracking, based on a previously developed method (Scherbaum et al., 2010) that lasts approximatively 8 minutes. During this task, participants have to respond to a series of arrows based on the direction of the arrow and ignoring its location. To respond they need to click on the response box corresponding to the direction of the arrow (left or right). In incongruent trials, the location of the arrow and its direction are different, which requires participants to inhibit the automatic response associated with the location of the stimulus and instead respond based on the location of the response box. This requires participants to engage in inhibitory control and overcome the interference (i.e., response conflict) caused by the irrelevant spatial information. This method allowed to track changes in the participant’s thought process during decision-making (Resulaj et al., 2009) and to identify specific time intervals leading to decision-making (Resulaj et al., 2009).
Behavioral measures include trajectories of mouse movements and reaction times. Neural activity is recorded throughout the task using electroencephalography (EEG).
Behavioral and neural data are analyzed at the trial level using linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models ((G)LMMs), accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data (trials nested within participants) and variability in the number of observations across groups. Neural analyses focus on response-locked midfrontal theta power and stimulus-locked N2 and P3 aplitudes as indexes of cognitive conflict. Behavioral analyses examine frequency of inhibition failures, mouse trajectories and neural markers using the same set of predictors, including congruency, session, and group (incoming, outgoing).
data_collection_procedures As part of this study, incoming detainees, outgoing detainees, and community control participants will be recruited. Incoming participants will consist of newly detained prisoners, selected from weekly lists of individuals newly received into custody in French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. Outgoing participants will consist of prisoners approaching release. During recruitment periods, we will aim to approach all eligible detainees and invite them to participate, with recruitment timing adapted to institutional and logistical constraints.
Community control participants will consist of first-year psychology students from Ghent University, recruited via the SONA system. Control participants will complete the same task at each timepoint and will receive course credits for their participation.
Prisoners will be excluded if they were transferred from other establishments, are scheduled for deportation or awaiting extradition (incoming group), or if they have insufficient understanding of Dutch or French, present visual or motor impairments, or exhibit inappropriate behavior toward the researcher.
Baseline assessments (T1) will take place in prison, three to seven weeks after incarceration for incoming participants and prior to release for outgoing participants. Follow-up testing sessions will be conducted at 4 (T2) and 8 months (T3) after baseline assessment. Control participants will be assessed at the first 2 sessions only (4-month re-test).
At each assessment, comprehensive contact information will be collected, reviewed, and updated for detainees, including residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and, when available, social media contact details. Participants will also be asked to provide contact information for alternative contacts (e.g., family members or friends), and to provide consent for these contacts to be used in case follow-up is required and their personal contact information has changed.
Participants will not be excluded based on the presence of mental disorders at recruitment. However, if participants are unable to complete the task or are non-compliant, they may be excluded from the analyses.
Participants will receive compensation for their participation. Incoming detainees will be compensated via their prison bank account. Outgoing participants will be compensated via bank transfer. Control participants will receive course credits for their participation at each timepoint.
sample_size The final target sample size for this study across all groups (control, incoming and outgoing) is approximatively 30 total participants completing the full study. Considering the high rates of attrition in studies involving prisoners with long periods of follow-up (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), we seek to recruit 300 incoming and 300 outgoing participants for the baseline assessment. For the control group we only seek to recruit 60 participants at baseline.
sample_size_rationale The target sample size was determined based on a series of a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007), reflecting the different components of the study design.
First, a power analysis was conducted for the incarcerated groups only, including incoming and outgoing detainees. This analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 2 groups and 6 repeated measurements, reflecting the combination of the 3-level session factor and the 2-level congruency factor. For detecting a medium effect size (f = .25), with 95% power, the required total sample size was estimated at 28 participants (i.e. 14 per group).
Second, an additional power analysis included the community control group for additional analyses of practice effects. Because control participants were assessed at two sessions, this analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 3 groups and 4 repeated measurements, corresponding to the 2-level session factor and the 2-level congruency factor. Under the same assumptions, the required total sample size was estimated at 45 participants (i.e. 15 per group).
However, this project is part of a larger study for which, keeping all other factors constant, an additional power analysis was conducted focusing on within-subject effects across 3 sessions, with 2 conditions (i.e. each task of the study includes at least 2 conditions), and was performed separately within each detainee group. This analysis yielded a required sample size of 28 participants per group.
Given the high attrition expected in longitudinal prison research, substantially larger samples are recruited at baseline to ensure sufficient statistical power at follow-up.
measured_variables • The primary behavioral outcome variable is the choice, operationalized as the frequency of inhibition failures in congruent and incongruent trials.
• The second behavioral outcome variable include mouse trajectories measures. AUC will be used as the primary spatial measure, as it captures the overall deviation of the mouse trajectory from the ideal path to the correct response. As such, it provides a continuous index of attraction toward the competing (incorrect) response option (Hehman et al., 2015). Compared to total distance travelled, AUC is less sensitive to general motor variability and more directly reflects response conflict (Stillman et al., 2018; Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020).
• In addition to this spatial index, we will include a complementary temporal measure of mouse-tracking trajectories (i.e. time spent moving toward the incorrect/opposite response option). This measure captures the duration of competition between response alternatives, providing insight into the temporal unfolding of response selection and conflict resolution processes (Freeman & Ambady, 2010; Scherbaum & Dshemuchadse, 2020).
• At the neural level, stimulus-locked ERP components will be examined, focusing on N2 and P3 amplitudes. Specifically, N2 and P3 responses will be quantified following stimulus and compared between congruent and incongruent trials; and across sessions.
• In addition, theta-band power will be assessed using EEG. Theta activity will be around the time of participants’ responses (response-locked). Analyses will compare theta power as a function of trial type (congruent vs. incongruent) and across sessions.
• Reaction time (RT) will be included as a covariate in the analyses, as an index of decision processes (e.g., conflict or deliberation), rather than as a primary outcome variable.
• Demographic variables will be collected, including age, gender, level of education, nature of the offense(s) leading to incarceration, length of incarceration, past criminal records, and socio-economic status.
• Personality and mental health measures will be included by means of self-reported questionnaires. Participants will rate each item based on its applicability over the preceding four weeks.
• For incarcerated participants, perception of the prison environment will be assessed at baseline using the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ; Bosma et al., 2020), a validated instrument measuring perceived prison conditions and social relationships within the institution.
• Following release (from T2 onwards), quality of life will be assessed using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ; Harper et al., 2021), which is adapted to measure well-being and life conditions outside the prison environment.
indices Indices of inhibitory control will be derived from mouse-tracking data.
AUC will be calculated for each trial as the area between the observed trajectory and an ideal straight-line trajectory from start to target box, providing an index of spatial attraction toward the competing response box.
The time spent moving toward the incorrect/opposite response option will be computed, capturing the duration of competition between response alternatives.
For both measures, effects of response conflict will be assessed by comparing incongruent and congruent trials, such that larger AUC values and longer time spent moving toward the incorrect response option reflect greater interference.
statistical_tests We will analyze the dependent variables using mixed-effects models to account for the repeated-measures structure of the data and the hierarchical organization of trials nested within participants.
Behavioral outcomes will be analyzed at the trial level using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) with a binomial link function. For the main confirmatory analysis, fixed effects will include Group (2-level), Session (3-level), Congruency (2-level), and their interactions. For the practice effect analysis, fixed effects will include Group (3-level), Session (2-level), Congruency (2-level), and their interactions.
Neural outcomes (theta band power, N2 and P3 amplitudes) will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). Fixed effects will include Group, Session, Congruency, and their interactions.
For both behavioral and neural analyses, covariates will include reaction time (RT), age, and questionnaire-derived measures (e.g., PCQ, GLQ, mental health, personality), as well as relevant demographic variables such as gender, education level, socioeconomic status, criminal history, and characteristics of the offense.
Random effects will include participant-level random intercepts, as well as random slopes for within-subject factors (e.g., Session and Congruency), where appropriate to capture individual variability in longitudinal changes and decision processes.
When significant main effects or interactions are observed, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using estimated marginal means (EMMs), with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Tukey adjustment).
Model assumptions will be assessed through standard diagnostic procedures, including inspection of residual distributions and evaluation of model fit.
transformations Raw EEG data will be preprocessed. We will use a Biosemi 32-electrode EEG system with four external electrodes. Two of the external electrodes will be placed on the left and right mastoids. Data will be acquired using ActiveView software, and subsequently converted to BIDS format. To filter and clean the data, we will use MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013). The data will be re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST). For time–frequency analyses, data will be band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz. Since our participants will not be placed in a Faraday Cage, we will apply a Notch filter to remove the power line noise at 50 Hz. To remove ocular and muscular artifacts, Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Artifact-related components will be identified using a combination of automatic classification and visual inspection of component topographies and time courses, and subsequently removed.
inference_criteria We will use the standard p<.05 criteria to determine the statistical significance of the ANOVA and post-hoc tests results. The post-hoc tests will be corrected for multiple comparisons using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustment approach.
data_exclusion_criteria Outliers will be identified at the trial level using a within-participant 2-of-3 rule, combining three criteria: median absolute deviation (MAD > 3), z-score (|z| > 3), and interquartile range (IQR beyond 1.5 × IQR). Trials flagged by at least two of these criteria will be excluded from subsequent analyses.
EEG data will be excluded when excessive artifacts are present. Artifact rejection will be based on a combination of automated detection procedures and visual inspection. Trials contaminated by noise (e.g., due to eye movements, muscle activity, or signal instability) will be removed. Participants contributing an insufficient number of valid trials after preprocessing will be excluded from EEG analyses.
exploratory_analyses In the case where some prisoners are released before the end of the data collection period, their available data will be retained and analyzed within a within-subject longitudinal framework.
In addition, in the case where some ex-prisoners re-offend before the end of the data collection period, baseline data from these participants may be used in exploratory analyses to identify potential predictors of reoffending.
Scores on questionnaires assessing mental health, personality, and quality of life in and outside prison (assessed using the PCQ and GLQ, respectively) will be compared over time to evaluate the effects of incarceration and time spent in prison on these factors.
paper_id input

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of deviations from preregistrations, see:

van den Akker O, Bakker M, van Assen M, Pennington C, Verweij L, Elsherif M, Claesen A, Gaillard S, Yeung S, Frankenberger J, Krautter K, Cockcroft J, Kreuer K, Evans T, Heppel F, Schoch S, Korbmacher M, Yamada Y, Albayrak-Aydemir N, Wicherts J (2024). “The potential of preregistration in psychology: Assessing preregistration producibility and preregistration-study consistency.” Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000687.

For educational material on how to report deviations from preregistrations, see:

Lakens, Daniël (2024). “When and How to Deviate From a Preregistration.” Collabra: Psychology, 10(1), 117094. doi:10.1525/collabra.117094.
